claims_made_by_source.claim: Ubik's described substance closely matches ubiquinone (CoQ10) in name (from Latin 'ubique') and in effects — anti-aging, anti-fatigue, wound healing, relief of heart-failure symptoms — properties documented in studies published 20–40 years after Ubik was written in 1966.
Ubiquinone was named in 1957 by R.A. Morton (University of Liverpool) and was unknown to the general public until CoQ10 reached the US market in 1983.

PKD almost certainly could not have known about ubiquinone: interviews with three ex-wives and a girlfriend found no biochemistry knowledge or contacts; the 1966 Britannica he owned does not mention it (the 1967 edition does, post-dating Ubik); only one obscure 1960 Scientific American citation existed.

Sarill was a personal friend and houseguest of PKD, is acknowledged in A Maze of Death, and as a physics grad student discussed Ubik's pseudo-scientific rationale with Dick, who never indicated it was based on real science.

Other reported PKD precognitions: the Flow My Tears Kathy/Jack/police-inspector match (1970–72); a trance diagnosis of his son's incarcerated hernia (confirmed by Tessa); and a Feb 25 1975 hypnagogic vision of a body in the exact position his own was found in seven years later.

The 2-3-74 onset: a delivery woman's golden-fish necklace triggered a pink-beam phosphene and anamnesis; PKD then felt taken over by an entity he called VALIS (Vast Active Living Intelligence System), with a feminine 'A.I.' voice seeming to come from a satellite.
Sarill proposes bipolar disorder (plus a sodium-pentothal rebound) as a likelier frame than the schizophrenia (Kinney) or temporal-lobe-epilepsy (Pickover) explanations.

Sarill concedes the precognition reading is not proof: Ubik 'provides synchronistic evidence consistent with precognition, not proof of it,' and a coincidence reading (Ubik as a divine/ubiquitous principle, as PKD himself glossed it in the Exegesis) remains available.
